input.instructions: Create a compact, accurate blueprint for an 8-to-12-minute educational lesson with exactly ten sequential teaching beats. Do not write full narration. Create exactly three measurable learning objectives. For every beat, provide one distinct complete factual claim, a concrete example, a concise editable visual direction, and one or two exact supplied source IDs. End the claim, example, and visual direction with complete punctuation. Every cited source excerpt must directly support the claim; reuse at least two important technical terms from each cited excerpt so support can be checked locally. Do not invent course assignments, policies, measurements, datasets, instruction encodings, or product behavior that is absent from the supplied excerpts. Keep the claim, example, and visual direction compact; a deterministic local expander will produce the full narration. Sequence the beats from foundations through application and end with a practical analysis checklist. Use only the supplied source excerpts for factual claims. Every factual claim must cite one or more supplied source IDs. Narration must describe information that is essential to understand visuals. Do not imitate a named creator or invent sources.
input.prompt:
Topic: CSCI-541: Programming Skills. Create a representative course-foundations companion aligned to the official catalog description. It must teach durable concepts and problem-solving methods without claiming to replace the instructor's syllabus. Official catalog description: The goal of this course is to introduce the students to a programming paradigm and an appropriate programming language chosen from those that are currently important or that show high promise of becoming important. A significant portion of the learning curve occurs through programming assignments with exemplary solutions discussed later in class. The instructor will post specifics prior to registration. With the approval of the program coordinator, the course can be taken for credit more than once, provided each instance deals with a different paradigm and language. Prerequisites: CSCI-344 or equivalent course. Contact Hours: Lecture 3 Typically Offered: Fall, Spring

Source excerpts:

[llvm-language-reference]
LLVM IR is a typed, SSA-based intermediate representation with explicit instructions, basic blocks, functions, memory operations, and control flow. A module contains global values, functions, declarations, and metadata. A function contains basic blocks, and every basic block ends with a terminator instruction. Phi instructions select values according to the predecessor control-flow edge. Load and store instructions make memory access explicit. Valid IR must satisfy structural and typing rules. The verifier reports IR that violates those rules. Compiler work separates parsing and semantic analysis from lowering, verification, optimization, and target-specific code generation.

[python-language-reference]
The Python language reference specifies lexical analysis, data model behavior, execution, expressions, statements, functions, classes, exceptions, and module import semantics. Python objects have identity, a type, and a value. Names are bound to objects within namespaces and scopes. Expressions produce values, while statements control execution and bindings. Exceptions interrupt normal control flow until a matching handler processes them or they propagate. The import system searches for modules and binds loaded modules into a namespace. Programs should be reasoned about through explicit state, control flow, data representation, contracts, tests, and observable behavior. Debugging separates syntax, runtime, and logical failures, while decomposition and abstraction reduce the number of interacting concerns.

[rit-csci-541]
The goal of this course is to introduce the students to a programming paradigm and an appropriate programming language chosen from those that are currently important or that show high promise of becoming important. A significant portion of the learning curve occurs through programming assignments with exemplary solutions discussed later in class. The instructor will post specifics prior to registration. With the approval of the program coordinator, the course can be taken for credit more than once, provided each instance deals with a different paradigm and language. Prerequisites: CSCI-344 or equivalent course. Contact Hours: Lecture 3 Typically Offered: Fall, Spring

beats.claim: CSCI-541 introduces a programming paradigm and a currently important or promising language to build durable problem-solving skills.
beats.example: Students might explore object-oriented programming in Python or functional concepts in Rust, depending on the instructor's selection.
beats.title: Course Scope and Paradigm Introduction
beats.visualDirection: Display a slide with the course title, paradigm/language options, and a note that specifics are posted prior to registration.

beats.claim: Official language references specify lexical analysis, data model behavior, execution, expressions, statements, functions, classes, exceptions, and module import semantics.
beats.example: The Python reference documents how names are bound to objects within namespaces and scopes, and how expressions produce values while statements control execution.
beats.title: Language Reference Structure
beats.visualDirection: Show a diagram of a language reference document with callouts for 'lexical analysis', 'data model', 'execution', and 'module import semantics'.

beats.claim: Python objects have identity, a type, and a value, and names are bound to objects within namespaces and scopes.
beats.example: A variable assignment like `x = 10` binds the name `x` to an integer object with a specific identity and value in the current scope.
beats.title: Object Identity and Namespaces
beats.visualDirection: Illustrate two boxes labeled 'Namespace' and 'Scope', with arrows pointing to object boxes showing 'identity', 'type', and 'value' attributes.

beats.claim: Exceptions interrupt normal control flow until a matching handler processes them or they propagate, while statements control execution and bindings.
beats.example: A `try-except` block catches a `ValueError` during input parsing, preventing the program from crashing and allowing recovery.
beats.title: Control Flow and Exceptions
beats.visualDirection: Draw a flowchart showing normal execution path, an exception trigger, a handler block, and a propagation path if no match exists.

beats.claim: The import system searches for modules and binds loaded modules into a namespace, enabling code reuse across files.
beats.example: Running `import math` loads the math module and binds its functions into the current namespace for direct access.
beats.title: Import System Mechanics
beats.visualDirection: Show a file system tree with a 'modules' folder, an arrow pointing to a namespace box, and a label indicating 'search path' and 'binding'.

beats.claim: Compiler work separates parsing and semantic analysis from lowering, verification, optimization, and target-specific code generation.
beats.example: Source code is first parsed into an abstract syntax tree, then semantically analyzed, lowered to intermediate representation, verified, optimized, and finally compiled to machine code.
beats.title: Compiler Phases and Separation of Concerns
beats.visualDirection: Create a horizontal pipeline diagram with five stages: 'Parsing', 'Semantic Analysis', 'Lowering', 'Verification/Optimization', 'Code Generation', with arrows connecting them.

beats.claim: LLVM IR is a typed, SSA-based intermediate representation with explicit instructions, basic blocks, functions, memory operations, and control flow.
beats.example: An IR function contains basic blocks where each block ends with a terminator instruction, ensuring explicit control flow paths.
beats.title: Intermediate Representation Basics
beats.visualDirection: Render a simplified IR snippet showing a function with two basic blocks, a terminator instruction at the end of each, and a phi instruction at the start of a merge block.

beats.claim: Phi instructions select values according to the predecessor control-flow edge, enabling correct value tracking across branching paths.
beats.example: A phi instruction at the start of a block merges different variable values depending on whether the loop condition was true or false.
beats.title: Phi Instructions and Control Flow
beats.visualDirection: Draw a diamond-shaped control flow graph with two incoming edges labeled 'True' and 'False', and a phi instruction at the merge point selecting values based on the edge.

beats.claim: Load and store instructions make memory access explicit, and valid IR must satisfy structural and typing rules, with the verifier reporting violations.
beats.example: A store instruction writes a value to a specific memory address, and the verifier checks that the type matches the memory location before execution.
beats.title: Memory Operations and Verification
beats.visualDirection: Show a memory map with labeled addresses, a 'store' instruction pointing to an address, and a 'verifier' icon highlighting a type mismatch error.

beats.claim: Debugging separates syntax, runtime, and logical failures, while decomposition and abstraction reduce the number of interacting concerns.
beats.example: A developer uses a debugger to isolate a runtime error in a function, then refactors the code into smaller modules to simplify testing.
beats.title: Debugging and Decomposition Strategies
beats.visualDirection: Display a checklist graphic with three categories: 'Syntax', 'Runtime', 'Logical', each with a checkbox and a brief description of what to look for.

learningObjectives: Define the core components of a programming language reference and explain how they map to program execution.
Explain how intermediate representations (IR) and source code relate to compiler phases and verification.
Apply debugging and decomposition strategies to isolate syntax, runtime, and logical failures in code.

input.text: Apply Import System Mechanics to a worked situation instead of treating it as an isolated definition. The import system searches for modules and binds loaded modules into a namespace. Consider this worked case: Running `import math` loads the math module and binds its functions into the current namespace for direct access. On screen, show a file system tree with a 'modules' folder, an arrow pointing to a namespace box, and a label indicating 'search path' and 'binding'. Work from the concrete inputs to the result, checking units, types, or invariants at each step. The worked case shows both how to apply the method and how to check it.

Next, compare the choices involved in Control Flow and Exceptions and make the decision criteria explicit. Exceptions interrupt normal control flow until a matching handler processes them or they propagate. Consider this worked case: A `try-except` block catches a `ValueError` during input parsing, preventing the program from crashing and allowing recovery. On screen, draw a flowchart showing normal execution path, an exception trigger, a handler block, and a propagation path if no match exists. Compare alternatives against the same constraints so the evaluation does not move the goalposts. Using shared criteria turns a preference into a defensible technical choice.

With the foundation in place, examine how Object Identity and Namespaces operates in a concrete sequence. Names are bound to objects within namespaces and scopes. Consider this worked case: A variable assignment like `x = 10` binds the name `x` to an integer object with a specific identity and value in the current scope. On screen, illustrate two boxes labeled 'Namespace' and 'Scope', with arrows pointing to object boxes showing 'identity', 'type', and 'value' attributes. Follow every arrow in order and name the state before and after each transition. The trace converts an abstract statement into an inspectable sequence.

Use Phi Instructions and Control Flow to diagnose a failure by separating symptoms, causes, and corrective action. Phi instructions select values according to the predecessor control-flow edge. Consider this worked case: A phi instruction at the start of a block merges different variable values depending on whether the loop condition was true or false. On screen, draw a diamond-shaped control flow graph with two incoming edges labeled 'True' and 'False', and a phi instruction at the merge point selecting values based on the edge. Locate the first point where observed behavior diverges from expected behavior, then test the smallest plausible cause. The diagnosis is strongest when another person can reproduce the observation and the test.

Now define Language Reference Structure precisely enough that another learner could test the definition. The Python language reference specifies lexical analysis, data model behavior, execution, expressions, statements, functions, classes, exceptions, and module import semantics.
